questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: What is the distinction between parsing and chunking?
options: Parsing embeds document text, while chunking fetches the original source bytes
Parsing rebuilds a whole document representation, while chunking picks retrieval units
Parsing preserves PDF coordinates, while chunking discards every layout mapping
Parsing and chunking are one stage, since retrieval units come straight from bytes

questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: Why should immutable source bytes be retained?
options: Because retaining bytes removes the need to record any parser version at all
Because the stored bytes prove the extracted text is semantically correct
Because keeping the bytes makes character offsets into the source text unnecessary
Because a new parser can rebuild and be compared against the same exact input

questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: What should a parser emit instead of silently returning empty text after failure?
options: An explicit failed or partial artifact carrying an error class and diagnostics
A success artifact whose extracted text field is set to a single empty string
A random fallback string so that downstream length checks continue to pass
A duplicate of the source identifier so that the record can be reprocessed later

questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: Why preserve page, block, or bounding-box mappings?
options: To raise the number of MinHash components each document signature can hold
To let the chunker split documents into fixed windows without any tokenizer
To trace normalized text back to the exact evidence in the source document
To let the pipeline delete the original source file once extraction finishes

questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: Which signal can expose a parser upgrade that drops most content?
options: A rise in the number of documents whose parse ended in the quarantine queue
A change in the media types the fetcher reports for newly crawled documents
An increase in the average wall-clock time each document takes to parse
A sharp fall in the ratio of extracted text size to the original source size

questions.topic: Parsing and Extraction as Pipeline Stages
questions.question: Why should untrusted document parsing run with strict resource limits and isolation?
options: Because parsers allocate no memory of their own once limits have been applied
Because a malformed input can exhaust resources or exploit the format handler
Because isolation is what guarantees the extracted text is semantically accurate
Because resource caps are what make language identification models more accurate

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: Which similarity does MinHash estimate?
options: The edit distance between the two documents' normalized character streams
The Euclidean distance between the two documents' weighted feature vectors
The Jaccard similarity between the two documents' sets of shingles
The ratio of the two documents' lengths after boilerplate has been removed

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: What distance is commonly compared between SimHash signatures?
options: Hamming distance, the number of bit positions at which the signatures differ
Jaccard distance, computed over the two documents' complete shingle sets
Manhattan distance, summed over the per-word counts in each document
Levenshtein distance, taken between the two signatures rendered as hex strings

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: If 102 of 128 MinHash components match, what is the estimated Jaccard similarity?
options: Approximately 0.797
Approximately 0.203

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: What is a tradeoff of using larger shingles?
options: They increase accidental overlap between unrelated documents in the corpus
They remove template boilerplate before the signature is ever computed
They convert a MinHash signature into a SimHash signature automatically
They demand longer exact runs of text and tolerate small edits less well

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: Why can two contradictory documents appear near-duplicate?
options: Because MinHash ignores the shared text and scores only the differing spans
Because they can share extensive template and vocabulary despite one crucial difference
Because SimHash compares only the canonical source URL of each document
Because the verification stage only compares document lengths once a bucket matches

questions.topic: MinHash and SimHash for Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.question: Why can symmetric Jaccard miss a short document copied inside a long compilation?
options: Because the intersection of their shingle sets is empty whenever lengths differ
Because MinHash cannot hash the individual words a short document contains
Because the large union shrinks the overlap fraction despite high containment
Because SimHash is the only signature that can detect containment relationships

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: What is LSH used for in near-duplicate pipelines?
options: To parse source documents into the shingle sets that signatures are built from
To generate likely-similar candidate pairs without comparing every pair
To assign each duplicate cluster the canonical record that survives filtering
To produce a final semantic label for each pair with complete certainty

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: When do two MinHash signatures become candidates under banding?
options: When every one of their signature component values differs across all bands
When their two documents have the same extracted length after normalization
When one signature has a numerically larger component than the other one
When all rows of at least one band are identical between the signatures

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: What is the candidate probability for similarity s, b bands, and r rows?
options: s divided by b times r
s raised to b plus r
b * r * s

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: What happens when banding uses more bands with fewer rows?
options: Both the recall and the number of candidate pairs generated fall sharply
Both the recall and the number of candidate pairs that are generated generally rise
The S-curve threshold moves higher, so only near-identical pairs collide
The verification stage becomes unnecessary because bucket matches are then exact

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: With b=20, r=5, and s=0.8, what is the approximate candidate probability?
options: Approximately 0.9996
Approximately 0.0475
Exactly 0.8
Approximately 0.3277

questions.topic: LSH: Finding Near-Duplicates Without All-Pairs Comparison
questions.question: Why should a new shingling version use a new LSH namespace?
options: Because a namespace is what determines the language routing of each document
Because an LSH index cannot be rebuilt once its buckets have been populated
Because every shingling version produces the same hashes for the same text
Because mixing incompatible signatures makes bucket collisions meaningless

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: Why should language ID store confidence and model version?
options: Because short or mixed-language text is uncertain and the models keep on changing
Because the confidence score is what determines the document's extracted length
Because a stored model version can stand in for the document's source identifier
Because a language label assigned once will never need to be revisited later

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: What is the purpose of filter reason codes?
options: To hide rejected documents from reviewers so the corpus report stays simple
To guarantee that every filtering rule treats each source domain identically
To make retention rates and false-positive review auditable per rule
To replace the version identifiers that each filtering rule would otherwise need

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: Why can one punctuation threshold harm corpus quality?
options: Because a punctuation ratio cannot be computed before the parser has finished
Because code and mathematical text legitimately carry many symbol characters
Because punctuation counts are unstable until exact deduplication has been run
Because a threshold applied per language cannot be versioned in the manifest

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: Why run exact deduplication before expensive quality models?
options: Because quality classifiers require duplicate copies to calibrate their scores
Because exact hashing also detects every near-duplicate the corpus contains
Because deduplication rewrites the language labels the router later depends on
Because it avoids paying for repeated inference on byte-identical content

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: How should a quality classifier trained on polished articles be audited?
options: By measuring false rejection and retention across languages and groups
By keeping only the documents that receive the classifier's highest scores
By applying it across the whole corpus at once and reviewing nothing further
By removing the confidence values so a single hard label drives every decision

questions.topic: Language ID and Quality Filtering
questions.question: What is the safe way to deploy changed filter thresholds?
options: Mutate the single existing corpus gradually so consumers see no break
Delete the lineage of rejected items so the new rule cannot be second-guessed
Build a versioned candidate corpus, compare distributions, then publish it
Apply the new rule directly and measure only the size of the resulting corpus
